page_title: What Is Structured Logging? Benefits and Tips

summary.title: What Is Structured Logging? Examples, Benefits, and Best Practices
summary.one_liner: Structured logging writes logs as consistent key-value fields (often JSON) instead of free text, so they can be searched, filtered, aggregated and correlated automatically.
keywords: how to write json logs in java node.js python
takeaways: Structured logs store each detail (timestamp, event, user_id, ip_address) as its own field, so tools can query them without fragile text parsing.
Java (Log4j2 JsonLayout), Node.js (Pino) and Python (python-json-logger) examples show how to emit JSON logs.
Use consistent field names, JSON format, and a standard schema across services.
Include contextual metadata such as service name, request ID, trace ID and severity, but never log passwords, tokens or personal data.
Centralizing structured logs in a platform like SigNoz enables field-based search, dashboards, alerts and trace correlation.
summary.summary: The article explains structured logging as writing application logs as machine-readable key-value fields, usually JSON, and contrasts it with free-form text logs using a failed-login example. It shows code examples in Java with Log4j2 JsonLayout, Node.js with Pino, and Python with python-json-logger, plus a CloudWatch Logs Insights query over JSON fields. It then covers how structure improves analysis, aggregation and correlation in microservices, followed by best practices such as consistent naming, contextual metadata, avoiding sensitive data, and appropriate log levels. It ends by suggesting centralizing logs in SigNoz or via the OpenTelemetry Collector.
